title: Die drei Handwerksburschen
source: Brüder Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmärchen, Band 2, 7. Auflage (Ausgabe letzter Hand), Dieterich, Göttingen 1857, KHM 120. Text from Wikisource (twice proofread against the original). 1857 spelling preserved (daß, gieng, Noth, that, thun, gethan). The 1857 edition prints this tale without paragraph breaks; the paragraphing here is editorial, added for readability. The wording is unchanged.
about: KHM 120 follows three penniless journeymen who strike a bargain with the Devil: seven years of fine clothes and easy money, on condition that they answer every question afterward with the same three set phrases — "we all three," "for money," and "and that was right." When the formulas nearly hang them for a murder they did not commit, the very words meant to damn them are what save their lives.

sentences.t: Es waren drei Handwerksbursche, die hatten es verabredet auf ihrer Wanderung beisammen zu bleiben und immer in einer Stadt zu arbeiten.
sentences.l: There were three journeymen, who had agreed to stay together on their travels and always to work in one town.
sentences.i: There were once three journeymen who had agreed to keep together on their wanderings and always to work in the same town.
sentences.n: A Handwerksbursch is a young craftsman on his Wanderschaft — the years of tramping from town to town that lay between apprenticeship and mastership, which this tale simply takes for granted. In “die hatten es verabredet,” the “es” looks forward to the two infinitives that follow. The 1857 book prints this tale straight through, with no paragraph breaks at all; the divisions here have been added so the reader can follow it a scene at a time.

sentences.t: Auf eine Zeit aber fanden sie bei ihren Meistern kein Verdienst mehr, so daß sie endlich ganz abgerissen waren und nichts zu leben hatten.
sentences.l: At one time, however, they found no more earnings with their masters, so that at last they were quite ragged and had nothing to live on.
sentences.i: At one point, though, there was no more work to be had with their masters, so that in the end they were quite out at elbows and had nothing to live on.
sentences.n: “Verdienst” here is the noun der Verdienst — earnings, paid work — not the verb form ‘you earn.’ “abgerissen,” literally ‘torn off,’ is said of a person in rags. “nichts zu leben haben” is to have nothing to live on.

sentences.t: Da sprach der eine „was sollen wir anfangen?
sentences.l: Then the one said, “what are we to begin?
sentences.i: Then one of them said, “what are we to do?
sentences.n: “anfangen” in the sense ‘to set about, to do’: “was sollen wir anfangen?” is the ordinary German for ‘what are we to do?’ “sprach,” the preterite of sprechen, does duty for ‘said’ throughout these tales.

sentences.t: hier bleiben können wir nicht länger, wir wollen wieder wandern,
sentences.l: stay here we can no longer; we will take to the road again,
sentences.i: we cannot stay here any longer; we will go on the tramp again,
sentences.n: Fronting the infinitive (“hier bleiben können wir nicht länger”) throws the weight onto the staying. “wollen” here is not ‘want’ but plain intention, ‘we will.’ “wandern” is the journeyman’s technical word for going from town to town after work.

sentences.t: und wenn wir in der Stadt, wo wir hin kommen, keine Arbeit finden, so wollen wir beim Herbergsvater ausmachen daß wir ihm schreiben wo wir uns aufhalten, und einer vom andern Nachricht haben kann, und dann wollen wir uns trennen;“
sentences.l: and if in the town where we come to we find no work, then we will arrange with the lodging-house keeper that we write to him where we are staying, and each can have news of the other, and then we will part;”
sentences.i: and if we find no work in whatever town we come to, then we will arrange with the lodging-house keeper that we write and tell him where we are stopping, so that each can get news of the other, and then we will part company;”
sentences.n: “ausmachen” here is to arrange or settle a thing, not ‘to put out.’ “schreiben” is the plain verb, ‘to write.’ The Herbergsvater kept the journeymen’s hostel in a town and served as their post office and clearing-house, which is what makes the plan practical. “wo wir hin kommen” splits the compound wohin.

sentences.t: das schien den andern auch das Beste.
sentences.l: that seemed to the others also the best.
sentences.i: that seemed the best course to the others too.
sentences.n: “scheinen” here is ‘to seem,’ not ‘to shine’ — one preterite form serves both senses — and it takes the dative of the person to whom something seems.

sentences.t: Sie zogen fort, da kam ihnen auf dem Weg ein reich gekleideter Mann entgegen, der fragte wer sie wären.
sentences.l: They set off, and on the way a richly dressed man came toward them, who asked who they were.
sentences.i: They set off, and on the road a richly dressed man came to meet them, and asked who they were.
sentences.n: “entgegenkommen” takes the dative: ‘came toward them.’ “reich” here is the adverb ‘richly,’ not the noun das Reich, ‘kingdom.’ “wären” is subjunctive because the question is being reported rather than quoted.

sentences.t: „Wir sind Handwerksleute und suchen Arbeit: wir haben uns bisher zusammen gehalten, wenn wir aber keine mehr finden, so wollen wir uns trennen.“
sentences.l: “We are craftsmen and are looking for work: we have kept together until now, but if we find no more, then we will part.”
sentences.i: “We are craftsmen looking for work; we have kept together so far, but if we find no more of it, we shall part.”
sentences.n: “zusammen halten” is to hold together, keep company. “keine” stands alone for “keine Arbeit,” the noun left to be understood from the clause before.

sentences.t: „Das hat keine Noth,“ sprach der Mann, „wenn ihr thun wollt was ich euch sage, solls euch an Geld und Arbeit nicht fehlen;
sentences.l: “There is no need of that,” said the man, “if you will do what I tell you, you shall want for neither money nor work;
sentences.i: “There is no call for that,” said the man; “if you will do as I tell you, you shall want for neither money nor work;
sentences.n: “das hat keine Noth” is a set phrase, ‘there is no need for that, no cause to worry.’ “an etwas fehlen” is impersonal: literally ‘it shall not be lacking to you in money and work.’ “solls” is soll es; “Noth” keeps the 1857 -th- (modern Not).

sentences.t: ja ihr sollt große Herren werden und in Kutschen fahren.“
sentences.l: indeed you shall become great lords and ride in coaches.”
sentences.i: indeed, you shall become great gentlemen and ride about in carriages.”
sentences.n: “ja” at the head of a clause is an intensifier, ‘indeed, why.’ Riding in a coach is this tale’s shorthand for having risen in the world — and the coach will arrive, literally, at the end.

sentences.t: Der eine sprach „wenns unserer Seele und Seligkeit nicht schadet, so wollen wirs wohl thun.“
sentences.l: The one said, “if it does no harm to our soul and salvation, then we will readily do it.”
sentences.i: One of them said, “if it does our souls and our salvation no harm, then we will gladly do it.”
sentences.n: “schaden” takes the dative of what is harmed. “wenns” and “wirs” are wenn es and wir es, clipped as they were spoken. The bargain is being tested for the one thing that matters — and the answer that comes back is carefully not a denial.

sentences.t: „Nein,“ antwortete der Mann, „ich habe keinen Theil an euch.“
sentences.l: “No,” answered the man, “I have no part in you.”
sentences.n: “an jemandem Theil haben” is to have a share or a claim in someone. It is a true answer and a slippery one: he has no claim on these three, and he is about to say whose soul he does have a claim on. “Theil” keeps the 1857 -th- (modern Teil).

sentences.t: Der andere aber hatte nach seinen Füßen gesehen, und als er da einen Pferdefuß und einen Menschenfuß erblickte, wollte er sich nicht mit ihm einlassen.
sentences.l: But the other had looked at his feet, and when he there caught sight of a horse’s hoof and a human foot, he would not get involved with him.
sentences.i: But the second had been looking at his feet, and when he caught sight of a horse’s hoof and a human foot there, he wanted nothing to do with him.
sentences.n: The mismatched feet are the devil’s standing mark in these tales, and the reader is expected to know them a sentence before the text names him. “sich mit jemandem einlassen” is to have dealings with someone, generally to one’s cost.

sentences.t: Der Teufel aber sprach „gebt euch zufrieden, es ist nicht auf euch abgesehen, sondern auf eines anderen Seele, der schon halb mein ist, und dessen Maaß nur voll laufen soll.“
sentences.l: But the devil said, “content yourselves; it is not aimed at you, but at another’s soul, who is already half mine, and whose measure has only to run full.”
sentences.i: But the devil said, “set your minds at rest; it is not you that is aimed at, but another man’s soul; he is already half mine, and his measure has only to fill up.”
sentences.n: “gebt euch zufrieden” is sich zufrieden geben, to be satisfied and let a thing rest. “es ist auf jemanden abgesehen” means to have designs on someone. “der” and “dessen” are masculine and pick up “eines anderen,” the other man, not the feminine Seele. “sein Maß läuft voll” is the old image of guilt as a vessel filling to the brim; when it is full, judgment falls. The devil names his real target here, in the hearing of the reader — and the innkeeper has not yet walked on.

sentences.t: Weil sie nun sicher waren, willigten sie ein, und der Teufel sagte ihnen was er verlangte,
sentences.l: Because they were now safe, they consented, and the devil told them what he required,
sentences.i: Since they were safe now, they agreed, and the devil told them what he wanted of them,
sentences.n: “einwilligen” is separable: “willigten … ein.” “sicher” here means safe from him, not certain.

sentences.t: der erste sollte auf jede Frage antworten „wir alle drei,“ der zweite „ums Geld,“ der dritte „und das war Recht.“
sentences.l: the first was to answer to every question “we all three,” the second “for the money,” the third “and that was right.”
sentences.i: the first was to answer every question with “all three of us,” the second with “for the money,” the third with “and that was right.”
sentences.n: These three formulas are the whole machinery of the tale, and the 1857 text prints them in the same words each time. The third, “und das war Recht,” prints Recht with a capital — the noun, ‘justice, what is lawful’ — while everyone who hears it takes it for the ordinary adverb ‘right, proper.’ English cannot hold both at once; this translation keeps ‘and that was right’ at every occurrence.

sentences.t: Das sollten sie immer hinter einander sagen, weiter aber dürften sie kein Wort sprechen, und überträten sie das Gebot, so wäre gleich alles Geld verschwunden:
sentences.l: That they were always to say one after another, but further they might speak no word, and if they transgressed the command, then all the money would at once be gone:
sentences.i: That they were always to say one after another, and beyond it they might not speak a word; and if they broke the command, all the money would vanish on the instant:
sentences.n: “überträten sie das Gebot” is a conditional with no wenn, verb fronted, and in the subjunctive besides, because the whole condition is reported speech. “übertreten” is to transgress a rule; “hinter einander” is one after the other.

sentences.t: so lange sie es aber befolgten, sollten ihre Taschen immer voll sein.
sentences.l: but as long as they kept to it, their pockets were always to be full.
sentences.i: but so long as they kept to it, their pockets would always be full.
sentences.n: “befolgen” is to observe or keep to a rule. “sollten” reports what was promised rather than laying an obligation on them.

sentences.t: Zum Anfang gab er ihnen auch gleich so viel als sie tragen konnten, und hieß sie in die Stadt in das und das Wirthshaus gehen.
sentences.l: To begin with he gave them at once as much as they could carry, and bade them go into the town to such and such an inn.
sentences.i: To begin with he gave them straight away as much as they could carry, and told them to go into the town, to such and such an inn.
sentences.n: “heißen” with a bare infinitive means to bid or tell someone to do a thing. “in das und das Wirthshaus” — ‘this and that inn’ — is the storyteller’s way of not naming a place. “Wirthshaus” keeps the 1857 -th-.

sentences.t: Sie giengen hinein, der Wirth kam ihnen entgegen und fragte „wollt ihr etwas zu essen?“
sentences.l: They went in, the innkeeper came to meet them and asked, “do you want something to eat?”
sentences.n: “giengen” is the 1857 spelling of gingen. This is the first of the many questions the three will answer with their formulas, and the comedy depends on how well the answers happen to fit.

sentences.t: Der erste antwortete „wir alle drei.“ „Ja,“ sagte der Wirth, „das mein ich auch.“
sentences.l: The first answered, “we all three.” “Yes,” said the innkeeper, “that is what I think too.”
sentences.i: The first answered, “all three of us.” “Yes,” said the innkeeper, “that is just what I thought.”
sentences.n: The innkeeper hears the formula as a perfectly sensible reply — all three will eat — and answers it as one. “mein” is the verb meinen, ‘I think, I mean,’ not the possessive.

sentences.t: Der zweite „ums Geld.“ „Das versteht sich“ sagte der Wirth.
sentences.l: The second, “for the money.” “That goes without saying,” said the innkeeper.
sentences.n: “ums Geld” is um das Geld, ‘for money.’ “das versteht sich” is fixed — literally ‘that understands itself,’ i.e. of course, naturally.

sentences.t: Der dritte „und das war Recht.“ „Ja wohl wars Recht“ sagte der Wirth.
sentences.l: The third, “and that was right.” “Right indeed it was,” said the innkeeper.
sentences.n: The innkeeper echoes the third formula straight back, taking it for agreement about the paying. Here the capital in “Recht” keeps the noun in view while the innkeeper hears only the adverb.

sentences.t: Es ward ihnen nun gut Essen und Trinken gebracht, und wohl aufgewartet.
sentences.l: There was now brought them good food and drink, and they were well waited on.
sentences.i: Good food and drink were now brought them, and they were well waited on.
sentences.n: A passive with the dummy “es” holding the front slot and “ward” as its auxiliary — the older form of wurde, which builds the passive all through these tales. “aufwarten” is to wait on someone at table.

sentences.t: Nach dem Essen mußte die Bezahlung geschehen,
sentences.l: After the meal the payment had to be made,
sentences.n: “geschehen” is literally ‘to happen’: the German lets the payment happen rather than making anyone perform it, which suits a scene in which nobody will say a plain word.

sentences.t: da hielt der Wirth dem einen die Rechnung hin, der sprach „wir alle drei,“ der zweite „ums Geld,“ der dritte „und das war Recht.“
sentences.l: then the innkeeper held out the reckoning to the one; he said “we all three,” the second “for the money,” the third “and that was right.”
sentences.i: so the innkeeper held out the bill to the first of them, who said “all three of us,” the second “for the money,” the third “and that was right.”
sentences.n: “hinhalten” is separable, ‘to hold out.’ The formulas now answer a bill rather than a question and still come out sounding sensible — the tale is showing how far the trick will stretch before it turns.

sentences.t: „Freilich ists Recht,“ sagte der Wirth, „alle drei bezahlen, und ohne Geld kann ich nichts geben.“
sentences.l: “Of course it is right,” said the innkeeper, “all three pay, and without money I can give nothing.”
sentences.n: “freilich” is ‘to be sure, of course.’ The innkeeper has begun supplying the sense himself, reading each formula as a statement of ordinary business.

sentences.t: Sie bezahlten aber noch mehr als er gefordert hatte.
sentences.l: But they paid still more than he had demanded.
sentences.n: “fordern” here is to demand or ask a price, not ‘to summon before a court.’ Paying over the odds is what first marks them out — and what makes the money in their pockets known to the whole house.

sentences.t: Die Gäste sahen das mit an und sprachen „die Leute müssen toll sein.“
sentences.l: The guests looked on at it and said, “these people must be mad.”
sentences.n: “mit ansehen” is to look on at something as it goes on. “toll” is mad in the sense of crazed, not angry — and the word will be repeated at the moment the innkeeper needs someone to blame.

sentences.t: „Ja, das sind sie auch,“ sagte der Wirth, „sie sind nicht recht klug.“
sentences.l: “Yes, so they are,” said the innkeeper, “they are not quite in their right wits.”
sentences.n: “nicht recht klug” — recht is the adverb here, ‘not quite clever, not right in the head.’ The same spelling, capitalised as a noun, is what the third journeyman keeps saying, and the tale is quietly setting the two against each other.

sentences.t: So blieben sie eine Zeit lang in dem Wirthshaus und sprachen kein ander Wort als „wir alle drei, ums Geld, und das war Recht.“
sentences.l: So they stayed a while in the inn and spoke no other word than “we all three, for the money, and that was right.”
sentences.i: So they stayed on for a time in the inn and spoke no other word than “all three of us, for the money, and that was right.”
sentences.n: “ander” with no ending is an older form (modern anderes). The three formulas are printed here in one breath, as the household must by now have heard them.

sentences.t: Sie sahen aber, und wußten alles was darin vorgieng.
sentences.l: But they saw, and knew everything that went on inside.
sentences.i: But they saw and knew everything that went on in the house.
sentences.n: “vorgieng” is the 1857 spelling of vorging, from separable vorgehen, ‘to go on, take place.’ This flat little sentence is the hinge of the tale: the silence that looks like idiocy is exactly what makes them witnesses.

sentences.t: Es trug sich zu, daß ein großer Kaufmann kam mit vielem Geld, der sprach „Herr Wirth, heb er mir mein Geld auf, da sind die drei närrischen Handwerksbursche, die möchten mirs stehlen.“
sentences.l: It came to pass that a great merchant came with much money, who said, “master innkeeper, keep my money for me; there are the three foolish journeymen, who might steal it from me.”
sentences.i: It came to pass that a rich merchant arrived with a great deal of money, and he said, “master innkeeper, keep my money by for me; those three foolish journeymen are here, and they might steal it from me.”
sentences.n: “sich zutragen” is ‘to come to pass.’ “heb er … auf” is aufheben, to keep or put by, in the old third-person form of address — one spoke to a social inferior as “er,” ‘let him do this,’ where we would say ‘you.’ It is a small piece of contempt, and it is aimed at the man who will kill him before morning.

sentences.t: Das that der Wirth. Wie er den Mantelsack in seine Stube trug, fühlte er daß er schwer von Gold war.
sentences.l: That the innkeeper did. As he carried the portmanteau into his room, he felt that it was heavy with gold.
sentences.i: That the innkeeper did. As he carried the travelling-bag into his own room, he felt how heavy it was with gold.
sentences.n: A Mantelsack is the roll or bag strapped behind a rider’s saddle for his cloak and belongings. “schwer von Gold” — heavy with gold; German uses von where English says with.

sentences.t: Darauf gab er den drei Handwerkern unten ein Lager, der Kaufmann aber kam oben hin in eine besondere Stube.
sentences.l: Thereupon he gave the three craftsmen a bed downstairs, but the merchant came up above into a separate room.
sentences.i: Thereupon he gave the three craftsmen a bed downstairs, while the merchant was put up above in a room of his own.
sentences.n: “ein Lager” is a place to lie, a bed made up on the floor; the word is plainer than Bett and suits what three penniless-looking journeymen would be given. “besondere” here is ‘separate, apart,’ not ‘special.’

sentences.t: Als Mitternacht war und der Wirth dachte sie schliefen alle, kam er mit seiner Frau, und sie hatten eine Holzaxt und schlugen den reichen Kaufmann todt;
sentences.l: When it was midnight and the innkeeper thought they were all asleep, he came with his wife, and they had a wood-axe and struck the rich merchant dead;
sentences.n: “schliefen” is subjunctive: what the innkeeper thought, reported. “todt schlagen” is a fixed pair, to strike dead, and “todt” keeps the 1857 -th-. The 1857 text spends one clause on the murder and not a word on horror.

sentences.t: nach vollbrachtem Mord legten sie sich wieder schlafen.
sentences.l: after the murder was accomplished they lay down to sleep again.
sentences.i: the murder accomplished, they lay down to sleep again.
sentences.n: “nach vollbrachtem Mord” is a compressed dative phrase — literally ‘after accomplished murder’ — the kind of thing German builds with a participle where English needs a clause. “sich schlafen legen” is to lie down to sleep.

sentences.t: Wies nun Tag war, gabs großen Lärm, der Kaufmann lag todt im Bett und schwamm in seinem Blut.
sentences.l: When it was now day, there was a great outcry; the merchant lay dead in the bed and swam in his blood.
sentences.i: When day came there was a great outcry: the merchant lay dead in his bed, swimming in his own blood.
sentences.n: “Wies” and “gabs” are wie es and gab es, clipped. “in seinem Blut schwimmen” is the set phrase for a body lying in a pool of its own blood; the German keeps the verb ‘to swim,’ and so does the literal line.

sentences.t: Da liefen alle Gäste zusammen, der Wirth aber sprach „das haben die drei tollen Handwerker gethan.“
sentences.l: Then all the guests ran together, but the innkeeper said, “the three mad craftsmen have done this.”
sentences.n: “zusammenlaufen” is to come running together, to gather in a crowd. The innkeeper has been preparing this accusation since the guests first called the three mad — and the tale let the reader watch him prepare it.

sentences.t: Die Gäste bestätigten es, und sagten „niemand anders kanns gewesen sein.“
sentences.l: The guests confirmed it, and said, “no one else can have been it.”
sentences.i: The guests bore him out, and said, “it can have been no one else.”
sentences.n: “kanns gewesen sein” is kann es gewesen sein, a perfect infinitive under a modal, built exactly as English builds ‘can have been.’

sentences.t: Der Wirth aber ließ sie rufen und sagte zu ihnen „habt ihr den Kaufmann getödtet?“
sentences.l: But the innkeeper had them called and said to them, “have you killed the merchant?”
sentences.n: “ließ sie rufen” — lassen with an infinitive: he had them summoned without doing it himself. “getödtet” keeps the 1857 -th- (modern getötet).

sentences.t: „Wir alle drei“ sagte der erste, „ums Geld“ der zweite, „und das war Recht“ der dritte.
sentences.l: “We all three,” said the first; “for the money,” the second; “and that was right,” the third.
sentences.i: “All three of us,” said the first; “for the money,” the second; “and that was right,” the third.
sentences.n: This is where the joke turns over. The three formulas are unchanged, and against this question they read as a full confession — to the deed, to the motive, and to a claim that the deed was just. Everything now depends on their not adding a syllable.

sentences.t: „Da hört ihrs nun,“ sprach der Wirth, „sie gestehens selber.“
sentences.l: “There you hear it now,” said the innkeeper, “they confess it themselves.”
sentences.n: “hört” is the second person plural, ‘you hear.’ “gestehens” is gestehen es. The innkeeper needs no evidence beyond words he has been listening to for weeks.

sentences.t: Sie wurden also ins Gefängnis gebracht, und sollten gerichtet werden.
sentences.l: So they were brought into prison, and were to be judged.
sentences.i: So they were taken off to prison, and were to be tried and sentenced.
sentences.n: “richten” in this legal sense covers both passing the sentence and carrying it out, which is why the tale can move from the courtroom to the scaffold in a single line.

sentences.t: Wie sie nun sahen daß es so ernsthaft gieng, ward ihnen doch angst,
sentences.l: When they now saw that it was going so much in earnest, fear came upon them after all,
sentences.i: When they saw that it was all in such deadly earnest, they grew afraid after all,
sentences.n: “ward ihnen angst” is impersonal with a dative — ‘it became fearful to them,’ i.e. they grew afraid. “doch” concedes the point: for all their bargain, they were frightened.

sentences.t: aber Nachts kam der Teufel und sprach „haltet nur noch einen Tag aus, und verscherzt euer Glück nicht, es soll euch kein Haar gekrümmt werden.“
sentences.l: but at night the devil came and said, “only hold out one more day, and do not throw your luck away; not a hair of yours shall be bent.”
sentences.i: but in the night the devil came and said, “only hold out one day more, and do not throw your good fortune away; not a hair of your heads shall be harmed.”
sentences.n: “aushalten” is separable: “haltet … aus,” hold out. “verscherzen” is to forfeit a thing by one’s own folly. “es soll euch kein Haar gekrümmt werden” is a set phrase of reassurance, ‘not a hair of your head shall be harmed’ — from a speaker who gives it a second edge.

sentences.t: Am andern Morgen wurden sie vor Gericht geführt: da sprach der Richter „seid ihr die Mörder?“ „Wir alle drei.“
sentences.l: The next morning they were led before the court: there the judge said, “are you the murderers?” “We all three.”
sentences.i: The next morning they were brought before the court, and the judge said, “are you the murderers?” “All three of us.”
sentences.n: “am andern Morgen” is ‘the next morning’ — ander for ‘next’ again. The formula is unchanged, and against this question there is no other way a court could take it.

sentences.t: „Warum habt ihr den Kaufmann erschlagen?“ „Ums Geld.“
sentences.l: “Why did you kill the merchant?” “For the money.”
sentences.n: “erschlagen” is to strike down, to kill by a blow — precisely what the axe did, though not by their hands. The second formula supplies a motive as neatly as the first supplied the culprits.

sentences.t: „Ihr Bösewichter,“ sagte der Richter, „habt ihr euch nicht der Sünde gescheut?“ „Und das war Recht.“
sentences.l: “You villains,” said the judge, “did you not shrink from the sin?” “And that was right.”
sentences.i: “You villains,” said the judge, “had you no dread of the sin?” “And that was right.”
sentences.n: “sich einer Sache scheuen” governs the genitive — “der Sünde” — and means to shrink from a thing. Answering this question, the third formula stops being funny: it does not deny the deed, it declares it just.

sentences.t: „Sie haben bekannt und sind noch halsstarrig dazu“ sprach der Richter, „führt sie gleich zum Tod.“
sentences.l: “They have confessed and are stiff-necked into the bargain,” said the judge, “take them at once to death.”
sentences.i: “They have confessed, and are stiff-necked into the bargain,” said the judge; “take them straight to execution.”
sentences.n: “halsstarrig,” literally ‘stiff-necked,’ is a biblical word for obstinate impenitence, and it is the third formula that has earned it. “führt” is a plural imperative, an order to the officers of the court.

sentences.t: Also wurden sie hinausgebracht, und der Wirth mußte mit in den Kreiß treten.
sentences.l: So they were brought out, and the innkeeper had to step into the ring along with them.
sentences.i: So they were led out, and the innkeeper had to step into the ring with them.
sentences.n: “der Kreiß” (1857 spelling of Kreis) is the ring kept clear round a place of execution, inside which the accusers and witnesses stood. That the innkeeper is made to stand in it too is going to matter shortly.

sentences.t: Wie sie nun von den Henkersknechten gefaßt und oben aufs Gerüst geführt wurden, wo der Scharfrichter mit bloßem Schwerte stand,
sentences.l: As they were now seized by the hangman’s men and led up onto the scaffold, where the executioner stood with a bare sword,
sentences.n: The Scharfrichter was the sworn official headsman and the Henkersknechte his assistants; beheading with the sword was the ordinary form for a sentence of this kind. “bloßem Schwerte” is bare, i.e. drawn, and “Schwerte” keeps the old dative -e.

sentences.t: kam auf einmal eine Kutsche mit vier blutrothen Füchsen bespannt, und fuhr daß das Feuer aus den Steinen sprang, aus dem Fenster aber winkte einer mit einem weißen Tuche.
sentences.l: all at once there came a coach harnessed with four blood-red sorrels, and drove so that the fire sprang out of the stones, and out of the window someone waved with a white cloth.
sentences.i: all at once a coach came up, drawn by four blood-red horses, driving so hard that sparks sprang from the cobbles; and out of the window someone was waving a white cloth.
sentences.n: “Füchse” said of horses are chestnuts or sorrels — the same word as Fuchs, ‘fox,’ used of a red coat; “blutroth” pushes the colour beyond anything a living horse has, which is the first hint of who is inside. “daß das Feuer aus den Steinen sprang” is the standing image for a headlong pace, iron shoes striking sparks from the paving. A white cloth waved from a carriage was the recognised signal of a reprieve.

sentences.t: Da sprach der Scharfrichter „es kommt Gnade,“ und ward auch aus dem Wagen „Gnade! Gnade!“ gerufen.
sentences.l: Then the executioner said, “mercy is coming,” and there was also called out of the carriage, “Mercy! Mercy!”
sentences.i: Then the executioner said, “a pardon is coming,” and from the carriage too came the cry, “Mercy! Mercy!”
sentences.n: “Gnade” is mercy and, in a court, a pardon. The second half is an impersonal passive with “ward” — literally ‘and there was also called from the carriage,’ with no one named as the caller.

sentences.t: Da trat der Teufel heraus, als ein sehr vornehmer Herr, prächtig gekleidet und sprach „ihr drei seid unschuldig;
sentences.l: Then the devil stepped out, as a very distinguished gentleman, splendidly dressed, and said, “you three are innocent;
sentences.i: Then the devil stepped out, in the shape of a very great gentleman, splendidly dressed, and said, “you three are innocent;
sentences.n: He keeps the promise of the first scene to the letter: they were to become great lords and ride in coaches, and he arrives as one, in one. Nobody in the crowd looks at his feet.

sentences.t: ihr dürft nun sprechen, sagt heraus was ihr gesehen und gehört habt.“
sentences.l: you may now speak; say out what you have seen and heard.”
sentences.i: you may speak now; out with what you have seen and heard.”
sentences.n: “dürfen” is permission, not obligation — the bar on speech is lifted, not a duty imposed. “heraussagen” is separable, ‘to say out, to speak out.’

sentences.t: Da sprach der älteste „wir haben den Kaufmann nicht getödtet, der Mörder steht da im Kreiß“ und deutete auf den Wirth,
sentences.l: Then the eldest said, “we have not killed the merchant; the murderer is standing there in the ring,” and pointed at the innkeeper,
sentences.i: Then the eldest said, “we did not kill the merchant; the murderer is standing there in the ring,” and pointed at the innkeeper,
sentences.n: “deuten auf” is to point at. These are the first words of their own that the three have spoken since the bargain, and the whole length of the tale has been holding them back.

sentences.t: „zum Wahrzeichen geht hin in seinen Keller, da hängen noch viele andere, die er ums Leben gebracht.“
sentences.l: “for a token, go into his cellar; there hang many others still, whom he has brought out of their lives.”
sentences.i: “for proof, go down into his cellar; there hang many others besides, whom he has done to death.”
sentences.n: “zum Wahrzeichen” — as a token, as proof; the object produced as evidence is a standing device in these tales. “jemanden ums Leben bringen” is to kill, literally ‘to bring someone out of his life.’ One clause reveals that the murder the reader watched was not the first.

sentences.t: Da schickte der Richter die Henkersknechte hin, die fanden es, wies gesagt war, und als sie dem Richter das berichtet hatten, ließ er den Wirth hinauf führen und ihm das Haupt abschlagen.
sentences.l: Then the judge sent the hangman’s men there; they found it as it had been said, and when they had reported that to the judge, he had the innkeeper led up and his head struck off.
sentences.i: Then the judge sent the hangman’s men, and they found it as had been said; and when they had reported it to the judge, he had the innkeeper led up and his head struck off.
sentences.n: “wies gesagt war” is wie es gesagt war. “ließ … führen” and “ließ … abschlagen” both use lassen with an infinitive: he had it done. “das Haupt” is the elevated word for head, which is the word an execution gets.

sentences.t: Da sprach der Teufel zu den dreien „nun hab ich die Seele, die ich haben wollte, ihr seid aber frei und habt Geld für euer Lebtag.“
sentences.l: Then the devil said to the three, “now I have the soul that I wanted, but you are free and have money for your lifetime.”
sentences.i: Then the devil said to the three, “now I have the soul I wanted; but you are free, and have money for the rest of your days.”
sentences.n: “den dreien” is the dative of the numeral drei used as a noun, ‘the three of them’ — not a verb. “euer Lebtag” is an old fixed phrase, ‘your lifelong.’ The devil has told no lie anywhere in the tale: the soul he came for was the innkeeper’s, and the three were only ever there to fill his measure.

glossary.ausmachen: ausmachen — to arrange, settle, agree (separable aus-); also ‘to put out, extinguish’
glossary.bekannt: bekennen — confessed, owned up (past participle: sie haben bekannt); also bekannt, ‘known, familiar’
glossary.dreien: drei — three (dat. pl. of the numeral used as a noun; zu den dreien: to the three of them)
glossary.dürften: dürfen — were allowed to, might (3rd pl. past subjunctive)
glossary.essen: das Essen — food, the meal (nach dem Essen: after the meal); also essen, the verb ‘to eat’
glossary.frage: die Frage — question (noun; auf jede Frage antworten: to answer every question); also frage, the imperative of fragen
glossary.füchsen: der Fuchs — chestnut or sorrel horses (dat. pl.; the same word as Fuchs ‘fox,’ used of a red-coated horse)
glossary.führt: führen — lead, take (2nd pl. imperative: führt sie zum Tod; also 3rd sg. present, ‘leads’)
glossary.gefordert: fordern — demanded, asked (past participle; mehr als er gefordert hatte: more than he had asked); also ‘summoned before a court’
glossary.hab: haben — have (1st sg. present, short for habe); also hab, the imperative ‘have’
glossary.haltet: aushalten — hold out, endure (2nd pl. imperative: haltet … aus, separable aus-); halten alone: to hold, keep
glossary.heb: aufheben — keep, put by (imperative in ‘heb er … auf,’ the old third-person form of address); heben alone: to lift
glossary.hieß: heißen — bade, told (3rd sg. preterite with a bare infinitive: hieß sie gehen, bade them go); also hieß, ‘was called’
glossary.hört: hören — hear (2nd pl. present: da hört ihrs nun); also 3rd sg. ‘hears,’ and in ‘hört auf,’ stops
glossary.ja: ja — yes; also the particle ‘indeed, why’ at the head of a clause (ja ihr sollt: why, you shall)
glossary.maaß: das Maß — measure (1857 spelling of Maß; sein Maß läuft voll: his measure fills up, of guilt reaching its limit)
glossary.mein: meinen — mean, think (1st sg. present, short for meine; das mein ich auch: that is what I think too); also mein, ‘my’
glossary.recht: recht — right, properly, quite (adverb: nicht recht klug, not quite in his right wits); capitalised, das Recht — right, justice, the noun in the refrain “und das war Recht”
glossary.reich: reich — rich, richly (adjective and adverb; reich gekleidet: richly dressed); also das Reich, kingdom
glossary.sage: sagen — say (1st sg. present: was ich euch sage); also die Sage, a legend or rumour
glossary.sagt: sagen — say out (2nd pl. imperative, here heraussagen: sagt heraus); also sagt, ‘says’
glossary.schien: scheinen — seemed (3rd sg. preterite; das schien ihnen das Beste: that seemed to them the best); also ‘shone’
glossary.schreiben: schreiben — to write (infinitive); also das Schreiben, a written missive
glossary.trinken: das Trinken — drink (Essen und Trinken: food and drink); also trinken, the verb ‘to drink’
glossary.verdienst: der Verdienst — earnings, paid work (noun; kein Verdienst mehr finden: to find no more work); also verdienst, ‘you earn,’ from verdienen
glossary.weg: der Weg — way, road (auf dem Weg: on the road); also weg, the adverb ‘away’
glossary.zogen: ziehen — set off, moved on (3rd pl. preterite; zogen fort, from fortziehen); also zogen an, ‘put on’
